parsed.attack: A first-time landlord with one unit encounters an unfamiliar fixture perhaps twice a year, and their settled behaviour in that moment is to call a plumber and expense the invoice against rental income - the cost of not knowing is deductible, which is precisely why they have never bothered to build the record. The wedge asks them to do unpaid inventory work on a property they do not live in, before anything has gone wrong, in exchange for value that only arrives at the second incident; that is the same deferred-payoff structure that has kept home-inventory apps commercially dead for two decades despite insurers pushing them. The referral loop is worse: the kill metric expects 15 of 50 tradespeople to hand a landlord's photo record to a customer unprompted, and a plumber's incentive is the opposite - opacity about what is installed is how the callout gets rebooked. Nothing in the evidence shows a landlord asking for this; the two citations are a dead hardware box and a category of dead apps.
parsed.strongest_defence: One-unit landlords are being pushed into record-keeping by licensing, EPC and gas-safety regimes anyway, and the freemium tier costs them nothing to start; the photo is taken in thirty seconds at the tenancy handover they are already doing, so no new visit and no new habit is required.
parsed.verdict_reason: The audience can buy its way out of the problem with a deductible callout, so the record is a nice-to-have whose value arrives too late to drive the purchase.
